extracted.intended_audience: general public, law students, policy makers, and practitioners interested in U.S. patent law and biotechnology (gene-patenting)
extracted.subtask_description: Summarizes legal standards and precedents governing whether isolated human genes, cDNA, diagnostic methods, and related biotechnology claims are patent-eligible subject matter under U.S. law (35 U.S.C. §101). Focuses on the Myriad Supreme Court decision and its interaction with earlier cases (Mayo, Chakrabarty, Bilski).

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory patent-eligibility under 35 U.S.C. §101
rubrics_metrics.description: "This part of U.S. law describes what is patent-eligible: 'any new and useful process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter, or any new and useful improvement thereof'. If the invention falls under one of several excluding categories, however, including a 'naturally occurring article' (a defined term in the law), then it is not patent eligible."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use §101 as the threshold inquiry for eligibility; if claimed subject matter is a process, machine, manufacture, or composition of matter it is prima facie eligible, but the statute and case law exclude natural phenomena, laws of nature, and abstract ideas. Determine whether the claim falls into an excluding category before proceeding to other patentability inquiries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Product of nature doctrine (isolation does not suffice)
rubrics_metrics.description: "A naturally occurring DNA segment is a product of nature and not patent eligible merely because it has been isolated."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims to naturally occurring substances remain ineligible if the only difference from the native product is isolation/purification; courts will examine whether isolation changes the fundamental character or information of the natural product (Myriad: isolation of DNA did not).

rubrics_metrics.name: cDNA patent-eligibility (engineered, not naturally occurring)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Supreme Court held that "cDNA is patent eligible because it is not naturally occurring" and that complementary DNA "should be patent eligible, because it does not exist in Nature but rather was 'engineered by man'."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: cDNA (complementary DNA with introns removed) can be treated as patent-eligible subject matter because it is not identical to a naturally occurring DNA segment; courts may treat man-made modifications that create something not present in nature as eligible under §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: "Markedly different" test from Diamond v. Chakrabarty
rubrics_metrics.description: Diamond v. Chakrabarty used the test of whether a genetically modified organism was 'markedly different' from those found in nature to rule that genetically modified organisms are patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether the claimed subject matter is 'markedly different' in character from natural counterparts. The Federal Circuit applied this reasoning to find isolated DNA chemically distinct; however, Myriad clarifies limits when the information/content remains identical to the natural form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mayo v. Prometheus 'inventive concept' requirement for claims implicating natural laws
rubrics_metrics.description: In Mayo the Court ruled that certain claims implicating natural laws were not patentable because they lacked an 'inventive concept' and amounted to merely describing natural relations; steps that are well-understood, routine, conventional do not make the claim patent-eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For method or diagnostic claims that rely on natural laws or natural correlations, courts will look for an 'inventive concept' that adds significantly more than the natural law itself; routine or conventional steps cannot supply patentability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method/diagnostic claims as abstract mental processes (Bilski/In re Bilski line)
rubrics_metrics.description: Comparisons of DNA sequences were found to be 'abstract mental processes' under the Federal Circuit's In re Bilski decision and therefore not patent eligible; the district court found the diagnostic method claims to be mere thought processes that do not yield real-world transformations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a claimed method merely performs mental steps (e.g., comparing sequences, thinking/analysis) without real-world transformative steps or an inventive application, it risks being treated as an abstract, non-patentable process.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purified-and-isolated doctrine (historical standard)
rubrics_metrics.description: Historically, U.S. courts allowed patents on molecules when 'purified and isolated' from their natural environments (examples: aspirin, adrenaline, vitamin B12, prostaglandins); USPTO guidelines (2001) stated DNA molecules are eligible when isolated and purified or synthesized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the historical practice: purification/ isolation changed character of some claimed chemical compositions and supported patents. Myriad and subsequent decisions limited or overturned this doctrine for naturally occurring genetic information even if isolated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventive contribution requirement for product-of-nature-like compositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Judge Bryson (dissent below) applied Mayo-like reasoning to compositions: in cases where the claimed composition is nearly identical to a product of nature, ask whether the applicant has made an 'inventive' contribution beyond merely incidental changes; mere breaking of covalent bonds or routine isolation is insufficient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a composition claim is substantially the same as a natural product, courts will require evidence of inventive modifications or functional differences beyond routine manipulation to reach patent eligibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability of drug-screening assays versus other claims
rubrics_metrics.description: The Federal Circuit found assays to find drugs to treat cancer patentable and stated that drug screening claims were not seriously questioned prior to the case; the Supreme Court's focus on isolated DNA did not categorically foreclose drug-screening claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate drug-screening or screening assay claims on their own factual and claim limitations — they may be patentable if they do not claim only natural laws or abstract processes and include inventive, practical applications or transformations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope distinction: compositions vs information/applications
rubrics_metrics.description: The CAFC considered valid gene claims as directed toward 'compositions of matter' rather than toward information; the Supreme Court emphasized that it did not consider patents on new applications of knowledge about genes (applications might be patentable).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Differentiate between claims to physical compositions (molecules, engineered DNA) and claims to informational content or applications (diagnostic uses, methods). Applications or inventive uses of genetic information may be treated differently from claims that merely recite natural information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Routine, well-understood, conventional steps do not confer patentability
rubrics_metrics.description: The Court noted Myriad's processes used to isolate DNA 'were well understood, widely used, and fairly uniform' and thus were not at issue; similar language from Mayo emphasizes that conventional steps cannot supply the inventive concept needed for patent eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing claims, identify whether claimed steps are merely routine laboratory work; if so these steps generally cannot transform a claim involving natural phenomena into patentable subject matter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunctions and enforcement standards (eBay v. MercExchange)
rubrics_metrics.description: Myriad was unable to get preliminary injunctions per eBay Inc. v. MercExchange, L.L.C.; the case had enforcement and remedy implications beyond eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if a patent exists, obtaining remedies (injunctions) requires satisfying equitable standards under eBay; enforcement outcomes (injunctions, settlements) affect real-world exclusivity and access but are distinct from §101 eligibility analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clinical laboratory/medical practitioner exemption limits (35 U.S.C. §287(c) implication)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. §287(c) (exemptions of patent infringement for doctors) 'does not apply to the activities of any person... who is engaged in ... the provision of ... clinical laboratory services' — relevant because clinical pathologists performing testing are not covered by the physician exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider statutory exemptions' scope: even if clinicians believe they are exempt, laboratory services may fall outside the physician exemption, meaning enforcement of patents against diagnostic testing labs remains a legal risk absent other defenses.
